St Philip's Cathedral, Birmingham: Designed by the English Baroque architect Thomas Archer.
Originally built as a parish church in 1715 before becoming a cathedral in 1905.
Blackburn Cathedral: The cathedral's distinctive lantern tower was completed in 1969.
Although the parish church is medieval, it only became a cathedral in 1926.
Bradford Cathedral: Parts of the building date back to the 15th century.
Bristol Cathedral: Its eastern end is regarded as one of England's finest examples of a medieval hall church.
Founded as St Augustine's Abbey in 1140 before becoming a cathedral in 1542.
Canterbury Cathedral: The site where Archbishop Thomas Becket was murdered in 1170.
The seat of the senior bishop of the Church of England.
Carlisle Cathedral: Has England's largest surviving medieval stained-glass east window.
Originally founded as an Augustinian priory in 1122 before becoming a cathedral in 1133.
Chelmsford Cathedral: Its origins date back to the 15th-century parish church of St Mary.
Chester Cathedral: Originally a Benedictine monastery before becoming a cathedral in 1541.
Famous for its extensive medieval choir stalls with intricate carvings.
Chichester Cathedral: Its separate medieval bell tower is unusual among English cathedrals.
Coventry Cathedral: The modern cathedral was built beside the ruins of the medieval cathedral destroyed during the local Blitz in 1940.
The ruined old cathedral has been preserved as a symbol of peace and reconciliation.
Derby Cathedral: Its 64.8-metre (212-foot) tower was completed in 1725 to a design by James Gibbs.
The tower is home to a resident flock of peregrine falcons that has nested there since 2006.
Durham Cathedral: A UNESCO World Heritage Site together with nearby Castle.
It houses the shrine of St Cuthbert and the tomb of the Venerable Bede.
Ely Cathedral: Its famous octagonal lantern tower was built after the original Norman crossing tower collapsed in 1322.
It is nicknamed 'The Ship of the Fens' because of its prominent position above the surrounding flat landscape.
Exeter Cathedral: It has the longest uninterrupted medieval vaulted ceiling in the world.
Its two Norman towers are among the oldest surviving parts of the building.
Gloucester Cathedral: The tomb of King Edward II is located inside the cathedral.
Its cloisters were used as filming locations for the Harry Potter films.
Guildford Cathedral: Construction began in 1936 but was interrupted by the Second World War before being completed in 1961.
Built from handmade bricks, many of which were laid by volunteers from the local community.
Hereford Cathedral: Home to the medieval Mappa Mundi, the largest surviving medieval world map.
Also houses the Chained Library, one of the world's largest surviving collections of chained books.
Leicester Cathedral: King Richard III was reinterred in the cathedral in 2015 after his remains were discovered.
The church became a cathedral in 1927.
Lichfield Cathedral: The only medieval English cathedral with three spires, earning it the nickname 'The Ladies of the Vale'.
It contains one of the oldest surviving illuminated manuscripts in Britain.
Lincoln Cathedral: It was the tallest building in the world for over 200 years after completion of its medieval central spire.
The cathedral is famous for a carving, which has become a symbol of the city.
Liverpool Anglican Cathedral: The largest cathedral in Britain and the eighth-largest church building in the world.
Designed by Sir Giles Gilbert Scott, who won the design competition at the age of just 22.
St. Paul's Cathedral: Designed by Sir Christopher Wren following the Great Fire of London in 1666.
Its famous Whispering Gallery allows whispers to be heard clearly on the opposite side of the dome.
Manchester Cathedral: Originally a parish church before becoming a cathedral in 1847.
Renowned for its richly carved medieval choir stalls and misericords.
St Nicholas' Cathedral, Newcastle upon T: Its distinctive lantern tower has become one of cities best-known landmarks.
Norwich Cathedral: Has one of the tallest cathedral spires in England at 96 metres (315 feet).
Its cloisters are the largest monastic cloisters in England.
Christ Church Cathedral, Oxford: It is both a cathedral and a chapel.
The cathedral traces its origins to St Frideswide's Priory, founded in the 12th century.
Peterborough Cathedral: Queen Catherine of Aragon was buried in the cathedral in 1536.
Its striking west front is famous for its three enormous Gothic arches.
Portsmouth Cathedral: Originally the parish church of St Thomas before becoming a cathedral in 1927.
Its modern west end extension was completed in the 1990s, blending historic and contemporary architecture.
Ripon Cathedral: Its crypt was built by St Wilfrid in the 7th century and is one of the oldest surviving structures of any English cathedral.
The cathedral has maintained the ancient tradition of the [***] Horn, sounded nightly by the city hornblower.
Rochester Cathedral: Founded in AD 604, making it England's second-oldest cathedral.
Its Norman architecture includes one of the finest Romanesque facades in England.
St Albans Cathedral: Built on the site where Britain's first Christian martyr is traditionally believed to have been buried.
Its Norman tower is the only surviving 11th-century great crossing tower in England.
Salisbury Cathedral: Has the tallest church spire in the United Kingdom at 123 metres (404 feet).
Houses one of the four surviving original 1215 Magna Carta manuscripts.
Sheffield Cathedral: Originally a parish church before becoming a cathedral in 1914.
Contains the Shrewsbury Chapel, dating from the 16th century, built for the Earls of Shrewsbury.
Southwark Cathedral: Its origins date back to a church founded in the 12th century on the south bank of the Thames.
Southwell Minster: Famous for an exquisite medieval stone carvings in the Chapter House.
Although called a minster, it has served as the cathedral since 1884.
St Edmundsbury Cathedral: Its Millennium Tower was completed in 2005 using traditional medieval building techniques.
Truro Cathedral: One of only three cathedrals in the United Kingdom with three spires.
Built in the Gothic Revival style between 1880 and 1910.
Wakefield Cathedral: Its spire rises to about 75 metres (247 feet), making it the tallest in Yorkshire.
The parish church became a cathedral in 1888.
Wells Cathedral: Famous for its unique medieval scissor arches supporting the central tower.
Its astronomical clock, dating largely from the 14th century, is one of the oldest working clocks in the world.
Winchester Cathedral: The longest medieval cathedral in Britain, measuring approximately 170 metres (558 feet).
The novelist Jane Austen is buried in the cathedral's north aisle.
Worcester Cathedral: The cathedral contains the tomb of King John, who was one of the signatories of the Magna Carta.
Composer Edward Elgar is buried in the cathedral, close to the memorial window dedicated to him.
York Minster: Has the largest expanse of medieval stained glass in England, including the Great East Window.
The present Gothic cathedral was begun in the 13th century and completed in the 15th century.
